correctness.rationale: For norm-one harmonic h^1 the radial Poisson representation gives a unique boundary complex measure of total variation one. Its analytic and coanalytic n-th absolute coefficients are |μhat(n)| and |μhat(−n)|. Each ≤1, so equality of the sum 2 at all S is exactly simultaneous unit-modulus Fourier coefficients for frequencies L=±S. Polar decomposition dμ=u dρ gives u(t)e^(−iℓt)=c_ℓ ρ-a.e. Division by ℓ=n0 pins t to the coset of the subgroup annihilated by integer ideal generated by L−n0: d=gcd(2n0,{n−n0}), giving all and only phase-weighted nonnegative masses in the result, with maximum distinct pole number d. Quantitatively, ∫|u e^(−iℓt)−cℓ|²dρ=2(1−|μhat(ℓ)|)≤2ε; L² triangle, integer Bezout telescoping with B=sum|kℓ|, and 2sin(d dist(t,E)/2)≥2d dist(t,E)/π yield inequality (2), while ℓ=n0 yields (3). Nearest-point transport gives the bounded-Lipschitz bound (4) by Cauchy–Schwarz and phase Lipschitz n0. For μ_s=(δ1+δexp(is))/2 one has ε=(max S)²s²/4+O_S(s⁴) and best translated d-coset RMS distance s/2 for small s, proving the √ε order cannot be improved. No p>1 or total variation stability is claimed.
residual_risks: The custom script tests finite atomic distributions only; the arbitrary-measure assertion relies on the analytic proof, not numerical enumeration.
Constants depend on one chosen integer Bézout certificate B; they are not optimized, and estimates do not claim total-variation closeness.
The sharp example establishes the optimal exponent of geometric concentration, not best multiplicative constant or an independent sharpness statement for every metric in (4).

value.rationale: The recently sharp harmonic Hardy h1 coefficient endpoint asks a natural equality question not addressed by scalar sharpness examples. The theorem fully classifies simultaneous extremizers for any finite set of positive orders by a computable integer ideal d, demonstrates genuine multisource boundary Poisson extremizers (e.g. S={1,3}) and a contrasting single-pole regime (S={1,2}), and gives an explicit bounded-Lipschitz stability rate for all nearly saturating complex boundary measures. The two-atom family proves the exponent 1/2 is optimal. This is a motivated infinite-family arithmetic classification and quantitative rigidity fact, not merely an arbitrary tiny case or a slight numerical gain. Individual Fourier triangle equality, integer Bezout, and Cauchy–Schwarz steps are elementary; the contribution is their complete joint application to the sharp endpoint and quantitative geometry. The final statement is restricted to h1, finite S, and weak rather than total-variation distance.
residual_risks: No optimal multiplicative stability constants are proved and they may grow with S.
The work is a relatively elementary endpoint refinement; the value depends on its structural classification and sharp rate, not a new general Fourier theorem.
Unseen classical covering general theorem could overturn the originality/value judgment if found.
